findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council breached borrowing maturity indicator with 43% of debt due within 12 months versus 30% target, but has returned to compliance
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, the council held 43% of borrowing due to mature within 12 months, exceeding the 30% prudential indicator maximum. The council deliberately paused longer-term PWLB borrowing in March 2026 following treasury advisor Arlingclose guidance during elevated market volatility caused by the US/Israel war with Iran; 10-year PWLB rates had risen to 5.88% (from 5.13% at period start). The council instead used short-term local authority loans at 4.0-7.0%, accepting near-term refinancing risk to avoid locking in elevated long-term rates. Compliance has been restored by summer 2026 as market conditions improved.
findings.matters: High proportion of debt maturing within short periods creates refinancing risk and exposure to rate movements if loans must be rolled over; however this breach was a deliberate tactical choice during volatile markets and has been actively managed.
findings.figures: 43% of borrowing due within 12 months vs 30% target; PWLB 10-year rates 5.13% to 5.88%; Short-term LA loan rates 4.0-4.5% most of year, rising to 5.0-7.0% at year-end
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, 43% of the Council's borrowing was due to mature within twelve months.

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Non-treasury investment portfolio of £61.3m is generating -£2.6m negative cash income despite showing 7.68% book value returns
findings.detail: The council holds £61.3m in non-treasury investments including investment property (£27.0m) and subsidiary loans and equity (£34.4m). Net income is forecast at -£2,639k for 2026/27. Book value returns appear positive at 7.68% because they include unrealised property valuations; however the council discloses that net income figures exclude these unrealised gains. Negative cash is driven by development project loans (Otterpool Park LLP -£1,834k, Oportunitas -£310k) and property portfolio losses (-£495k), indicating the portfolio is in growth phase and not self-funding.
findings.matters: A £61m portfolio that is currently consuming cash (negative £2.6m annually) and relies on unrealised valuations for positive returns represents concentration risk; if property valuations fall or projects encounter delays, the portfolio could move to loss positions and further deplete reserves.
findings.figures: Total non-treasury investments £61.3m; Forecasted net income 2026/27 -£2,639k; Book value return 7.68%; Otterpool Park LLP -£1,834k; Oportunitas -£310k; Property -£495k
findings.quote: The net income and rate of return excludes the impact of any unrealised property valuation gains or losses.

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Otterpool Park LLP development loan increased to £23.8m and is currently generating -£1.8m negative annual cash income
findings.detail: The council has loaned £23.8m to Otterpool Park LLP (an increase of £2.5m from prior year £21.3m) as financing for the Otterpool Park Garden Town development. Total exposure including equity stake is £25.7m. The LLP is currently in development phase and generating negative cash returns, with net income forecast at -£1,834k for 2026/27, reflecting capital being deployed to acquire land and commence works rather than generate revenues. The council treats this as a long-term strategic investment expected to eventually generate returns as the development matures.
findings.matters: A £23.8m loan to a single development project that is currently negative cash-generative represents material development and counterparty risk; lenders need clarity on project viability and when the council will receive cash returns.
findings.figures: Otterpool Park LLP loan £21.3m → £23.8m (+£2.5m); Total exposure £25.7m (loan £23.8m + equity £1.9m); Forecasted 2026/27 net income -£1,834k

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement and borrowing increased 10% due to capital programme expansion, particularly Otterpool Park Garden Town
findings.detail: The council's capital financing requirement increased from £156.8m to £172.6m (+£15.8m or 10%) during 2025/26, driven by capital expenditure funded through prudential borrowing. Major contributors include Otterpool Park Garden Town development (£4.1m), HRA projects (£9.3m), Changing Tides (£0.8m), plus a £1.8m adjustment from MRP methodology changes. The council continued using internal borrowing against cash reserves.
findings.matters: A 10% year-on-year increase in the CFR and borrowing indicates accelerating debt-funded capital investment, which increases the council's long-term debt service obligations and sensitivity to future interest rate movements.
findings.figures: CFR increased £15.8m to £172.6m; Borrowing up £10.3m to £117.8m; Otterpool Park £4.1m; HRA £9.3m; Long-term borrowing up £13.3m

findings.matters: Leisure services are asset-intensive; ageing facilities combined with rising operational costs can become unsustainable. The council's need to commit capital to maintain these services indicates cost pressures are significant.
findings.figures: Risk score 9 (Significant/Likely); no specific capital budgets stated for facilities
findings.quote: Rising costs, staffing shortages, and ageing facilities threaten leisure service sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 2026_07_29_A&G Committe Report_Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Local Government Re-organisation creates extended strategic uncertainty affecting decision-making and project delivery
findings.detail: LGR is rated as a high risk (score 9). The council has appointed a programme director and project manager and is undertaking advance transition planning for new unitary councils. However, the risk register explicitly states LGR could disrupt decision-making, strategic projects and service delivery.
findings.matters: LGR introduces extended strategic uncertainty and transition risk for a council. This affects the council's ability to plan, finance and execute major projects and maintain service delivery stability through the transition period.
findings.figures: Risk score 9 (Significant/Likely); target score to reduce to 6
findings.quote: LGR disrupts decision-making, strategic projects, and service delivery.

findings.paper_title: 2026_07_29_A&G Committe Report_Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: EU-Entry/Exit system border checks create new operational risk; score escalated from 6 to 9
findings.detail: The council's EU-Entry/Exit system risk has escalated from 'Significant' (6) to 'Significant/Likely' (9) due to biometric checks rolling out at Dover Port and Eurotunnel. The register notes that first-time registrations may increase border processing times at peak periods, creating queues and congestion affecting residents, businesses, tourism, freight and council service delivery in a location where the council sits directly between Dover and Folkestone.
findings.matters: Operational disruption at the border directly affects council service delivery capacity and the local economy on which council finances depend.
findings.figures: Risk score increased from 6 to 9; 'Significant' x 'Likely'
findings.quote: First-time registrations may increase border processing times, particularly at peak periods, creating queues and congestion on routes serving Dover and Folkestone, with knock-on impacts for residents, businesses, tourism, freight movement and council service delivery.

findings.paper_title: 2026_07_29_A&G Committe Report_Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs escalating; £5M capital deployment required
findings.detail: The council faces a high-risk combination of increased demand and rising costs for temporary housing. In response, the council has identified additional HRA units and secured £5M of HRA funding to acquire accommodation. Re-procurement of the provider framework is planned for April 2027, suggesting the current arrangements are cost-pressured and need restructuring.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a growing cost pressure for councils nationally; this council is deploying significant capital to manage it, indicating cost escalation beyond routine management capacity.
findings.figures: £5M HRA funding secured to acquire TA units; risk score 9 (Significant/Likely)
findings.quote: Utlising £5M funding to acquire and supply TA units for use.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Receipts Position Statement 25_26, 30/06/2026 Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.headline: Contingency for urgent or unforeseen capital expenditure is only £500k, creating thin coverage for unexpected needs.
findings.detail: The council has set aside just £500k (3% of total receipts) as contingency for urgent or unforeseen capital expenditure, a small reserve to handle emergency repairs or cost overruns across the entire capital estate.
findings.matters: Combined with tight uncommitted receipts, this leaves the council with limited ability to respond to emergency capital failures without either finding new asset sales or cutting approved schemes.
findings.figures: Contingency £500k out of total receipts £16,783k
findings.quote: Contingency for urgent or unforeseen capital expenditure 500

findings.headline: HRA capital expenditure consumes 62% of committed capital receipts, indicating heavy concentration in housing investment.
findings.detail: £9.216m out of £14.851m committed capital receipts is allocated to HRA capital expenditure, more than seven times the General Fund capital allocation of £1.316m. This dominance of housing spending shapes the entire capital programme.
findings.matters: The concentration of nearly two-thirds of capital receipts in housing suggests either aging stock with substantial repair demands or HRA financial pressures that may constrain other council capital priorities.
findings.figures: HRA capital £9,216k, GF capital £1,316k
findings.quote: Committed towards HRA capital expenditure 9,216

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Receipts Position Statement 25_26, 30/06/2026 Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.headline: Uncommitted capital receipts of only £1.989m leave the council with minimal flexibility for new General Fund capital investment.
findings.detail: Of £16.8m total capital receipts (£11.818m brought forward plus £4.965m received in year), £14.851m is committed to existing and planned schemes. This leaves only £1.989m, or 12% of total receipts, uncommitted to support new General Fund capital expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender assesses capital flexibility as a measure of financial resilience; this tight position indicates the council cannot fund new capital priorities without generating additional asset sales, suggesting capital funding pressure.
findings.figures: Total receipts £16,783k, Committed £14,851k, Uncommitted £1,989k

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025.26 General Fund Outturn Reserves Analysis, 30/06/2026 Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.headline: Princes Parade capital project written off
findings.detail: The Financial Resilience Reserve was drawn for write-off of the Princes Parade Project. The reserve declined significantly from opening balance of £3.775m to closing balance of £205m, though the disclosure does not itemise the portion attributable to this write-off.
findings.matters: Capital write-offs indicate projects not completed or not delivering expected outcomes. They consume reserves that otherwise provide financial buffers and can signal execution risk across the capital programme.
findings.figures: Reserve declined from £3.775m to £205k overall; Princes Parade write-off amount not itemised
findings.quote: Drawdown for write off of Princes Parade Project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - 2025.26 General Fund Outturn Reserves Analysis, 30/06/2026 Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee
findings.headline: Homelessness Prevention reserve of £1.321m completely drawn for temporary accommodation subsidy gap
findings.detail: The Homelessness Prevention Reserve, which stood at £1.321m at the start of 2025/26, was entirely drawn during the year to cover a housing subsidy gap for temporary accommodation. The council shows no closing balance in this reserve. This was a one-off use of reserves to plug an ongoing funding shortfall.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs exceeding baseline funding is a structural problem. When a council exhausts an earmarked reserve in a single year for an ongoing service, it signals inadequate baseline funding and indicates the gap will need to be closed by service cuts or new revenue sources in future years.

findings.paper_title: Capital Provisional Outturn Report 25_26 JS
findings.headline: Capital programme relies on £5.012m borrowing to fund 31% of outturn expenditure
findings.detail: Of the £16.224m actual capital spend in 2025/26, £5.012m (31%) is financed by borrowing. Borrowing is concentrated in three schemes: Otterpool Park (£4.1m), Changing Tides leisure development (£762k), and waste vehicles (£150k). The council's prudential borrowing is expected to generate revenue benefits or capital receipts.
findings.matters: Material dependence on borrowing to finance capital programmes increases the council's debt burden and future revenue commitments for debt servicing; material to assessing prudential borrowing compliance and debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £5.012m borrowing out of £16.224m outturn; breakdown: Otterpool Park £4,100k, Changing Tides £762k, Waste Vehicles £150k
findings.quote: The outturn for the programme requires £5.012m of borrowing to support it.

findings.paper_title: Capital Provisional Outturn Report 25_26 JS
findings.headline: Storm Goretti damage to Mermaid Beach coastal defences requires unplanned £200k capital repair
findings.detail: The council suffered significant storm damage to its coastal sea defences at Mermaid Beach during Storm Goretti earlier this year. The damage has been assessed and will require repairs. This is an unplanned capital cost that will be added to the 2026/27 capital programme and funded from revenue carry forward.
findings.matters: Unplanned costs signal climate and weather resilience risks to the council's asset base and ability to forecast future capital needs; funding from revenue carry forward reduces reserves available for other purposes.
findings.figures: £200k repair cost to be added to 2026/27 capital programme
findings.quote: Significant damage was caused to the coastal sea defences at Mermaid Beach during Storm Goretti earlier this year. This has been assessed in order to understand the work necessary to repair the damage and the cost. This will be reported to Full Council separately to seek inclusion of the funding in the 2026/27 Capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Capital Provisional Outturn Report 25_26 JS
findings.headline: Otterpool Park project commits £4.1m borrowing with capitalised interest partially recoverable from Homes England partnership
findings.detail: The council is financing Otterpool Park, a major development project, entirely through borrowing (£4.1m). Interest costs incurred before the assets are ready for use are being capitalised against the capital budget rather than charged to revenue. A Collaboration Agreement with Homes England (February 2025) will recover up to £1.6m of historic project costs, reducing but not eliminating the council's exposure to this major capital commitment.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's debt burden needs to track major capital commitments and how costs are being managed, particularly where revenue costs are being deferred through capitalisation.
findings.figures: £4.1m borrowing for Otterpool Park; up to £1.6m cost recovery via Homes England reimbursement
findings.quote: some of the overall historic costs (up to £1.6m) of the Otterpool project will be reimbursed, having entered into a Collaboration Agreement with Homes England in February 2025 which will serve to reduce the overall project spend to the Council.

findings.paper_title: HRA Cabinet report - Revenue and Capital Provisional Final Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Multiple capital projects are experiencing delivery delays, and the council has identified insufficient capacity to manage both the £15.8m carry-forwards and the new 2026/27 capital programme as a medium-likelihood risk
findings.detail: Specific delays include: carbon improvement works (£627k, decarbonisation and delivery team capacity issues); Everist Court remodelling (£623k, planning and procurement delays); domestic gas heating (£256k, tendering delays); and Mittell Court IL schemes (£409k combined, commencement delays). The risk register explicitly flags that capacity to manage delayed expenditure alongside the new year programme is a medium likelihood risk.
findings.matters: Systemic delays across multiple programmes, coupled with an explicit capacity warning, indicate execution risk on delivering both the carry-forward and new investment in 2026/27. This could signal resource or procurement planning issues.
findings.figures: Multiple project delays totalling carry-forwards of £15,769k; capacity risk identified as medium-medium
findings.quote: The underspend in Carbon Improvement works is primarily due to delays associated with the decarbonisation project and challenges in securing sufficient delivery team capacity

findings.paper_title: HRA Cabinet report - Revenue and Capital Provisional Final Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Dwelling rental income was overestimated by £378k in the budget, with 44 new build properties at Risborough Barracks rescheduled to 2026/27, deferring revenue generation
findings.detail: Budgeted dwelling rental income of £21.1m was not achieved; actual was £20.7m. This £378k miss relates partly to rescheduling of 44 new build units at Risborough Barracks to 2026/27. Non-dwelling rental income also decreased by £60k due to lower garage occupancy. The council acknowledged these were forecasting errors during budget setting.
findings.matters: Rental income is the HRA's primary revenue source. A 1.8% overestimate signals forecasting challenges, and deferral of 44 units to next year means delayed revenue that was counted on for this period.
findings.figures: Dwelling rents £378k below budget; 44 properties rescheduled; non-dwelling rents £60k below budget; total rental income variance £442k
findings.quote: a decrease in dwelling rents of £378k due to an over estimation during the budget setting process, and rescheduling of 44 new build properties at Risborough Barracks to 2026/27

findings.paper_title: HRA Cabinet report - Revenue and Capital Provisional Final Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Nearly half the HRA capital programme (47% of budget) was re-profiled from 2025/26 to 2026/27, with £13.2m relating to new build and acquisition delays including Boundary Road, Pentland Homes and Risborough Barracks
findings.detail: The HRA Capital programme spent £17.8m against an approved budget of £33.8m. The largest variance (£13.2m) relates to new builds and acquisitions, with completion now expected in 2026/27. An additional £5m added for interim accommodation in late 2025 could not be spent before year-end. The council is carrying forward £15.8m of capital budget to the next financial year.
findings.matters: The scale of re-profiling indicates execution delays in housing delivery. This affects the pace at which the HRA can generate rental income from new assets and suggests delivery or procurement challenges that could recur.
findings.figures: £16.1m underspent of £33.8m budget; £13.214m new build/acquisition variance; £15,769k total carry-forwards
findings.quote: The HRA Capital programme has spent £16.1m less than the latest approved budget

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision methodology changed from straight-line to annuity, saving £2.2m in the outturn
findings.detail: In February 2026, full Council approved a change to how the council calculates its minimum revenue provision (MRP)—the amount it must set aside to repay borrowing. The change from straight-line to annuity saves £2.184m in this year's accounts. While approved and not improper, it is a technical accounting change that improved the outturn position rather than a genuine operational improvement.
findings.matters: MRP methodology changes are legitimate but represent a shift in how the council accounts for debt repayment. A lender should note that £2.2m of the 'favorable' position is from a one-off accounting treatment change, not from genuine operational improvement.
findings.figures: £2.184m favorable variance
findings.quote: Minimum Revenue Provision – (£2.184m) - favourable variance driven by a revision of MRP methodology from straight line to annuity, as approved by full Council in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Prices Parade Planning Project written off for £3.4m, though offset by use of Financial Resilience reserve
findings.detail: A capital project (Prices Parade Planning) was written off entirely this year with a loss of £3.4m. The council covered this from the Financial Resilience reserve, meaning it did not hit the outturn, but the reserve had to absorb a major capital failure.
findings.matters: Capital project failures are routine; having a reserve to absorb them is prudent. But a £3.4m write-off on a single project signals either poor planning, scheme failure, or overly optimistic initial estimates. It also depletes the reserve meant to cushion other shocks.
findings.figures: £3.4m written off
findings.quote: Corporate Estates & Development - £3.081m - unfavourable variance is driven mainly by the Prices Parade Planning Project being written off this year (£3.4m). This is offset by a planned transfer from the Financial Resilience reserve.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: £5.5m in unspent budget being carried forward to next year specifically to address forecast funding gaps
findings.detail: The council is holding £5.468m as carry forwards, described explicitly as needed to 'address forecast funding gaps' in 2026/27. This is a large proportion of annual movements and signals the council knows the coming year will have a structural funding shortfall it is pre-funding with this year's underspends and carried budget.
findings.matters: Forward carry forwards labelled against 'funding gaps' is a council's way of saying 'we do not have enough money next year and we are trying to avoid a deficit by holding this back.' It suggests deteriorating financial position and medium-term sustainability concerns.
findings.quote: provisional operational carry forwards of £5.468m have been approved by the Section 151 Officer and CLT as budgeted revenue expenditure relating to 2025/26 that will be carried forward to 2026/27 to reinvest in frontline services and address forecast funding gaps.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Service budgets overran by £3m, worsened by £650k since Q3, driven chiefly by temporary accommodation pressures
findings.detail: Service spend came in £3.034m worse than approved budget—not a small variance but a deterioration. It got £654k worse between Q3 and outturn. The primary driver is temporary accommodation, which appears across multiple service lines (Governance & Finance, Homelessness & Housing Options). The council's underlying service spending is not under control.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget shortfalls are one-off or structural. A deteriorating position between Q3 and outturn, driven by recurring demand (homelessness), signals the council cannot forecast or control costs in its core services.
findings.figures: £3.034m unfavourable variance on services; £654k deterioration from Q3
findings.quote: The overall spend against service budgets for the year has resulted in an unfavourable position of £3.034m (Appendix A, 'Total for Service'), a movement of £654k to Q3 projections, driven in large part by temporary accommodation pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Funding loss of £2.4m from Kent County Council discontinuing a support scheme, forcing the council to fund temporary accommodation costs from reserves
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £2.404m of income from rent rebates, housing benefits for temporary accommodation, council tax benefits and council tax reduction scheme, funded via Kent County Council. KCC discontinued the scheme mid-year. The council is now covering this gap using the Homelessness Prevention Grant reserve, revealing a significant and growing homelessness burden.
findings.matters: Loss of external funding combined with rising temporary accommodation need means the council is depleting reserves to meet a current demand that has no sustainable funding answer. This is a structural problem, not a one-off.
findings.quote: £2.404m of expenditure for rent rebates, housing benefits [temporary accommodation], council tax benefits and council tax reduction scheme budgeted income that is no longer being received; this is based on a Kent County Council decision to discontinue the scheme.

findings.paper_title: Folkestone Hythe District Council_Letter on 2025-26 Audit Timelines
findings.headline: New financial system implementation during 2026-27 audit and reporting period
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new financial system in 2026-27, coinciding with the period when audit deadlines are at their tightest. The auditors note they will coordinate to ensure the audit process works alongside the system implementation.
findings.matters: Financial system implementations carry inherent risks around data migration and control gaps that could affect the council's ability to close accounts and meet audit deadlines during a critical compliance period.

findings.quote: We recognise that you will be implementing a new financial system in 2026/27 and we will work with you to ensure that the audit process works in tandem with this process.

findings.headline: MHCLG assessing council's ability to maintain and rebuild assurance by 31 July 2026
findings.detail: Grant Thornton reports that MHCLG has requested a case-by-case assessment of whether Folkestone and Hythe can maintain and, where necessary, rebuild assurance. This assessment is due 31 July 2026 and is described as key to demonstrating the council's capability to meet the new audit deadlines.
findings.matters: The language 'rebuild assurance' signals MHCLG may have identified governance or audit concerns, and wants auditor confirmation the council can recover and meet tightened statutory deadlines.
findings.figures: Assessment due 31 July 2026
findings.quote: MHCLG have asked us as a firm to report by 31 July 2026, on a case-by-case basis, our assessment of the Council's ability to both maintain and where necessary rebuild assurance

findings.paper_title: Folkestone and Hythe DC Audit Findings Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £3.57m valuation error discovered and corrected in Oportunitas Ltd equity investment
findings.detail: The Council's wholly-owned subsidiary Oportunitas Ltd (providing affordable housing) was valued at £734k at March 2024. During 2025 valuation work, material errors were identified: the discount rate was incorrectly applied and applied to interim cash flows rather than full-year figures. The revised valuation is £4.3m, a £3.57m understatement. Corrected via prior period adjustment in 2025 accounts.
findings.matters: A five-fold valuation error indicates material weaknesses in the Council's asset valuation processes, particularly for complex unlisted investments. This raises questions about reliability of valuations across the asset base (£289.54m in land and buildings, council dwellings and investment properties).
findings.figures: Prior value £734k, corrected value £4.3m, error of £3.57m (material misstatement)
findings.quote: Correcting these inputs resulted in a revised fair value of £4.3m, meaning the investment was understated by £3.57m in the 2024 financial statements. This misstatement is material and qualifies as a prior period error.

findings.paper_title: Folkestone and Hythe DC Audit Findings Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £3.4m from Princes Parade development will be written off to revenue in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council capitalised £3.4m of costs for a Princes Parade development (housing and leisure centre) from April 2022. The project was paused in 2022/23 due to difficult economic conditions and formally ended following a public consultation in June 2025. The £3.4m remains on the balance sheet as assets under construction and the Council intends to write the entire amount to revenue in 2025/26, creating a material one-time charge.
findings.matters: A significant capital scheme has been wound down with full write-off to follow, indicating capital scheme management issues and creating material budget impact in the next financial year.
findings.figures: £3.4m capitalised costs brought forward from April 2023; represents 130% of materiality (£2.6m)
findings.quote: The development was initially capitalised as an asset under construction (AUC), with costs of £3.4m brought forward as at 1 April 2022/23 with management intending to write off this balance within the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Council has identified 'a number of demand-led budgets which are difficult to control' as a strategic risk
findings.detail: As part of budget assumptions, the council explicitly notes it is responsible for multiple demand-led budget areas that are 'difficult to control.' This is flagged as part of the strategic risk assessment that informed the council's minimum reserve levels.
findings.matters: Demand-led services (typically social care, housing support) are hard to forecast and control. Unplanned spending in these areas can quickly erode reserves. The council's explicit identification of this as a control risk is material to reserve adequacy and financial resilience.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The council is responsible for a number of demand -led budgets which are difficult to control.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: General Fund minimum reserve of £1.5m is contingent on delivering savings proposals over the planning period
findings.detail: Council sets minimum General Fund reserve at £1.5m based on strategic risk assessment. The policy states this minimum 'will be monitored and should be addressed as savings proposals are developed and implemented.' This makes reserve adequacy conditional on executing the council's savings plan.
findings.matters: If the council fails to deliver planned savings, it will face pressure either to cut deeper or to breach its own minimum reserve level. This signals that current reserve levels depend on successful delivery of savings proposals and suggests underlying financial pressure.
findings.figures: General Fund minimum £1.5m
findings.quote: This level will be monitored and should be addressed as savings proposals are developed and implemented over the term of this plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in progress; external auditors require reserves maintained prudently through transition
findings.detail: Council is undergoing LGR. Both central government and external auditors (Grant Thornton) have mandated that reserve usage cannot be changed as a result of LGR, and reserves must be maintained at prudent levels through reorganisation and by successor bodies.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change affecting the council's independence and future organisation. This constraint on reserve usage during transition is a lending risk factor and signals that both auditors and government are watching reserve discipline closely.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The guidance from both Central Government and external parties such as our external auditors Grant Thornton have been very clear in that the planned use of reserves, similar to the disposal of assets should not be changed as a direct result of LGR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Reserves reduced to 'adequate rather than excessive' level following major capital investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool
findings.detail: Council has deliberately drawn down reserves over recent years to fund capital investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool projects and other investments, or to reduce borrowing. The council now describes reserves as 'adequate rather than excessive' - meaning the financial cushion is tight and not excessive.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's cash buffer for absorbing unexpected pressures. Reserves at 'adequate rather than excessive' level means limited room to maneuver if new risks materialise or demand-led services overspend.
findings.figures: General Fund minimum £1.5m, HRA minimum £2.0m, Capital Receipts minimum £0.5m
findings.quote: The level of reserves has, in recent years, reduced in line with planned activities such as investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool and their use for other investment or in lieu of borrowing. This strategy means that reserves are currently at an adequate rather than excessive level

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council holds £27.1m in commercial property to generate revenue offsetting declining government funding, explicitly acknowledging exposure to market demand, void tenancy, and capital value risks
findings.detail: The council has invested £27.1m in commercial property (largest: Connect 38 in Ashford at £16.4m; Otterpool Park land £8.5m) with the explicit purpose of generating capital gains and revenue streams to replace declining government grants. The council acknowledges principal risks include 'fluctuations in future demand of the market including competition, risk of void tenancies, fall in capital values etc.'
findings.matters: The council has substituted declined grant funding with higher-risk commercial property investment as a revenue source. Market downturns, property voids, or capital value falls would directly reduce revenue available for service delivery.
findings.figures: £27.1m commercial investments; £16.4m Connect 38; £8.5m Otterpool Park land; net income £1.6m (2025/26 forecast)
findings.quote: With central government financial support for local public services declining, the Authority previously invested in commercial property and land with the intention of making capital gains or generating new revenue streams to spend on lol public services. Total commercial investments are currently valued at £27.1m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs rising to 14.2% of housing revenue by 2028/29, driven by 65% growth in housing capital financing requirement
findings.detail: HRA financing costs (interest and MRP on housing debt) are projected to rise from £1.9m in 2024/25 (9.2% of HRA revenue) to £3.5m by 2028/29 (14.2% of revenue). This is driven by the HRA capital financing requirement growing from £50.4m to £83.2m, a 65% increase, as the council accelerates capital investment in housing stock.
findings.matters: An increasing proportion of housing revenue consumed by debt service reduces resources available for repairs, maintenance, and service delivery. At 14.2% of revenue, debt service represents a significant operational burden.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: £1.9m (2024/25) to £3.5m (2028/29); proportion of revenue: 9.2% to 14.2%; HRA CFR: £50.4m to £83.2m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: External grant funding for capital projects fell 41% year-on-year, forcing increased reliance on debt to finance the capital programme
findings.detail: External sources (government grants and contributions) funding capital expenditure fell from £20.3m in 2025/26 forecast to £12.0m in 2026/27 budget. To maintain the £46.4m capital programme, the council increased debt financing from £14.4m to £20.1m, a 40% increase.
findings.matters: Declining grant-in-aid increases reliance on borrowed money to fund capital, raising debt service costs in future years. It signals reduced external support and forces debt-financed capital strategies.
findings.figures: External sources 2025/26: £20.3m; 2026/27: £12.0m (41% decline). Debt financing: £14.4m to £20.1m (40% increase)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development, the largest service investment, expected to generate no capital receipts over the next three years
findings.detail: Otterpool Park is the council's largest service investment (part of £34m total service investments), with £8.5m held in land and property and £4.6m capital expenditure budgeted for 2026/27. The council explicitly states no capital receipts are anticipated from the development over the three-year period to 2028/29.
findings.matters: A long-dated capital commitment with explicitly deferred or uncertain returns increases financial risk. If the development stalls, underperforms, or faces market headwinds, capital remains locked up in a non-productive asset during the forecast period.
findings.figures: £4.6m capital budget 2026/27; £8.5m land holding; £34m total service investments; £0 receipts anticipated to 2028/29
findings.quote: No capital receipts from Otterpool Park development are anticipated to be received over the three-year period to 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council switching minimum revenue provision from straight-line to annuity method, backloading debt repayment to later years
findings.detail: Following a review by advisors Arlingclose in 2025/26, the council has changed its MRP calculation method from straight-line to annuity. The annuity method produces lower charges in early years and higher charges in later years over a 50-year amortisation period. This change takes effect from 2025/26.
findings.matters: A lender assessing sustainability needs to understand the debt servicing trajectory. Annuity method defers charges to later years, backloading repayment obligations when the council's revenue position may be less certain.
findings.figures: Lower early charges, higher later charges; applied to assets with useful lives up to 50 years
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council engaged its advisors to undertake a review of the MRP. As a result of the review, it was recommended to change the MRP method from straight line to annuity; this means lower charges in the early years and higher charges in later years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs are uncertain but reserved; November 2025 deadline for MHCLG submissions
findings.detail: The council notes: 'proposals for reorganisation of local government remain ongoing with the other Kent authorities ahead of the November 2025 deadline for submissions to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. A Local Government Reorganisation reserve was set up in 2025/26 to help mitigate any costs associated with reorganisation.' LGR could reshape the council's cost base and structure.
findings.matters: LGR is a material uncertainty; the reserve indicates recognition of significant one-off and potentially recurring costs ahead. Reorganisation outcomes could change the council's financial profile and risk profile.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund reserves of £21.55m cannot bridge the structural deficit; reserves are one-time only
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'use of reserves is only a one -off (one year option) as it only reduces the shortfall for the year it is applied.' Total reserves at 1 April 2025 were £21.55m (General Reserve £5.89m). The council must solve the deficit through permanent baseline cuts or new recurring income, not reserves.
findings.matters: Finite reserves cannot bridge a multi-year structural deficit; this signals the council's reserves cannot be a crutch and that permanent solutions must be found. Reserve depletion signals financial stress.
findings.figures: Total General Fund reserves £21.55m; General Reserve £5.89m; policy minimum 10% of net cost of services
findings.quote: use of reserves is only a one -off (one year option) as it only reduces the shortfall for the year it is applied.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Pension fund triennial valuation due December 2025 with current assumption of no change—outcome uncertain
findings.detail: The council states: 'A new valuation is due in December 2025 from the pension fund actuary and will impact the 2026/27 budget. Current assumptions are no change to the pension contributions rate.' Pension valuations can significantly alter costs if funding levels or longevity assumptions move.
findings.matters: Pension contribution rate increases (often £0.5m–£2m+ for a council this size) would worsen the MTFS deficit; the assumption of no change is optimistic and a material risk.
findings.figures: Last valuation Nov 2022; new valuation due Dec 2025; current assumption zero change to contribution rate
findings.quote: A new valuation is due in December 2025 from the pension fund actuary and will impact the 2026/27 budget. Current assumptions are no change to the pension contributions rate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Pay award locks in £850k additional cost for 2026/27 on £21.6m payroll; future-year assumption of 2% may not hold
findings.detail: The council has a two-year pay settlement from April 2025. The second year (2026/27) allows £1,500 added to each salary point or 3.5%, whichever is greater, equating to 'approximately £850k.' The MTFS assumes only 2% pay growth for 2027/28 onwards, which is at risk if public-sector pay catch-up continues.
findings.matters: Pay awards are fixed costs that cannot flex when income shortfalls occur; underestimating future pay growth increases the deficit faster than currently forecast.
findings.figures: £850k cost of 2026/27 pay award on £21.6m payroll base; assumed 2% for 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: The second year of the agreement will feed into the 2026/27 budget setting process and allows for £1,500 to be added to every salary point on all salary scales or 3.5%, whichever is the greater amount. This equates to approximately £850k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation 'subsidy gap' is growing; Central Government funding does not match private-market costs
findings.detail: The council identifies this as a major ongoing pressure: 'there is an increased service demand for temporary accommodation nationwide. Where the Council utilises private lets for the purpose of temporary accommodation, central Government does not fully fund the cost of those placements creating the 'subsidy gap'.' The council is now considering capital investment in TA properties to minimize these losses.
findings.matters: TA costs are structural and volatile; the 'subsidy gap' represents a growing unbudgeted cost with no resolution until the housing crisis eases, and capital investment in TA properties represents a significant new commitment with uncertain returns.

findings.detail: The strategy assumes 'the LGFS will be 'cash flat' for district councils again this year, with no new funding or increase in core spending power.' This continues a pattern where Revenue Support Grant has effectively ceased (none 2018/19–2023/24) and new grants rolled in during 2025/26 were offset by removal of previous grants, creating no net gain.
findings.matters: With inflation running 3.6%–3.8% and pay awards locked at 3.5% minimum, a flat cash settlement forces real-terms service cuts or revenue-raising; this is a key driver of the MTFS deficit.

findings.detail: The council currently retains £4.1m from business rates (40% of £45m+ collected, after tariffs/top-ups). A Business Rates Reset consultation outcome is expected Nov 2025 or Dec 2025. findings.detail: The council received £0.432m NHB in 2025/26 to fund revenue. This is a permanent loss of income with no mitigation plan.

Partially offset by increased Revenue Support Grant but the net impact is loss of a volatile, discretionary revenue source.

The S151 Officer explicitly acknowledges the council 'has drawn on them in the last three years' and emphasizes 'reserves can only be applied once', signalling concern about the sustainability of continued drawdown.

The £2.88m in 2029/30 alone accounts for almost all of that year's £3.2m deficit, indicating the council has not identified savings to absorb these costs.
findings.matters: Contractual inflation creates uncontrollable cost pressures that are difficult to absorb through savings. The scale (£2.88m) and its concentration in the final year creates a cliff-edge budget risk. Services may be at risk if the council cannot find offsetting savings or income.

findings.detail: Interest payable and similar charges grow steadily from £3.09m (2025/26) to £3.76m (2029/30), an increase of £670k. This 22% growth in debt servicing costs occurs alongside the emerging funding gaps and suggests the council is borrowing to meet service needs or capital investment at the same time its revenue budget is under strain.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs add to future budget pressure precisely when the council faces a £5.4m cumulative deficit. Lenders need to understand whether further borrowing is planned to close the gap, and whether total debt levels remain sustainable given this fiscal tightness.

findings.detail: Other non-service related grants fall from £4.17m (2025/26) to £1.16m (2026/27), losing nearly £3m in one year. Revenue Support Grant drops from £5.98m (2026/27) to £4.94m (2027/28) and stabilizes at £3.86m. findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: A cumulative funding gap of £5.4m accumulates by 2029/30, with no identified funding source in this forecast.
findings.detail: The council forecasts balanced budgets in 2025/26 and 2026/27, but deficits emerge from 2027/28: £1.1m in that year, £1.1m in 2028/29, and £3.2m in 2029/30. The cumulative effect is £5.4m by the end of the MTFS period. The 2029/30 deficit is partly driven by £2.88m of contractual non-service inflation for which no mitigation is identified in this appendix.
findings.matters: A £5.4m accumulated deficit over four years means the council must make substantial service cuts, significantly raise council tax, or draw reserves down significantly. This indicates unresolved budget pressure and potential financial stress in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment income declining as proportion of budget while council increases borrowing to fund investments
findings.detail: The percentage of gross expenditure funded by investment income is forecast to drop from 5.9% in 2025/26 to 4.5% in 2026/27. Simultaneously, the amount of investments funded by borrowing is rising from £55.9m to £63.2m. Treasury management returns are also declining, forecast at 3.75% for 2026/27 versus 4.5% in 2025/26. This combination—rising leverage, falling yields, and declining proportional income—reduces the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: The council is increasing its debt-funded investment exposure at a time when those investments are returning less to support the General Fund budget, suggesting tightening finances and increased risk if market conditions deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Investment income proportion: 5.9% (2025/26) to 4.5% (2026/27); borrowing-funded investments: £55.9m (2025) to £63.2m (2027 forecast); treasury rate of return: 4.5% to 3.75%

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio shows £5.2m in losses with further write-downs anticipated
findings.detail: The council's investment property holdings are valued at £27.1m against a purchase cost of £32.3m, representing £5.2m in unrealized losses. Connect 38 Offices accounts for £1.5m of this loss (valued at £16.4m against £17.9m cost). A separate parcel of land has been written down entirely (£2.9m loss). findings.matters: Asset values below purchase cost signal deteriorating commercial property market conditions and reduce the security underpinning the investment portfolio. The flagged expectation of further write-downs in the audit process suggests management anticipates additional losses.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development will not contribute revenue to the council for at least five years
findings.detail: The council has loaned £24.0m and invested £1.8m equity in Otterpool Park LLP, a Garden Town scheme. The document explicitly states that no capital receipts or contributions are anticipated during the entire Medium Term Financial Strategy period to 2030/31. The council's future capital investment plans do not require repayment of the equity; instead, long-term modelling assumes the authority will recover its total investment from the scheme's projected net proceeds. This is a 30-year development with no near-term financial return.
findings.matters: A major investment (£25.8m total exposure) with no anticipated contribution to council finances for five or more years ties up capital and reduces flexibility during budget pressures. The council is borrowing to fund this investment, increasing leverage while returns remain distant and uncertain.

findings.headline: Balance sheet resources are forecast to decline by £17.7m through 2028/29 as the council draws down reserves to fund capital expenditure through internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council is using an 'internal borrowing' strategy, where it deploys cash balances and reserves to fund capital spending rather than raising external debt. However, available balance sheet resources are declining from £67.7m (2024/25) to £50.0m (2028/29). The document notes this drawdown will continue as the council uses reserves to meet approved capital expenditure plans and substitutes them for external borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and cushion against unexpected expenditure, and signal that the council will eventually need to rely more heavily on external borrowing

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development lacks a confirmed strategic partner, and the council is excluding anticipated capital contributions from its financial forecasts pending partnership negotiations
findings.detail: Otterpool Park is identified as a major capital project requiring future funding through borrowing, but the council's financial planning explicitly excludes any future capital contributions or receipts from the scheme. The council is currently exploring partnership arrangements to fund the project. This creates uncertainty around whether the full borrowing burden will fall on the council or whether a partner will share the financing.
findings.matters: A major capital development without confirmed external financing or partnership creates financial uncertainty and means the council is forecasting higher debt levels than may ultimately be needed

findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow significantly from £156.8m (2024/25) to £192.3m (2026/27). findings.figures: CFR growing from £156.8m (2024/25) to £192.3m (2026/27); borrowing forecast of £122.9m in 2026/27; additional borrowing £17.5m between 2025/26 and 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery remains a challenge with 20% underspend in 2024/25, partly driven by slippage on the Otterpool project.

findings.quote: In 2024/25, capital spend was approximately 20% under budget, a significant portion of which relates to the 'Folkestone – A Brighter Future' project. The Council should monitor delivery more closely to identify potential slippage and take corrective action.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Procurement practices show systemic weaknesses: waivers are routine, contract registers are incomplete, and contracts routinely expire before replacements are signed.
findings.detail: The council's procurement process relies on waivers driven by late engagement and minimal justification, exposing it to contractual risk. Contract management suffers from an incomplete register, inconsistent compliance, and no centralised supplier performance monitoring. Waivers were frequently required because contracts expired before new agreements were signed, forcing backdated agreements and reliance on supplier goodwill. These weaknesses have persisted for years and create non-compliance, financial exposure, and reputational risk.
findings.matters: Weak procurement controls mean the council may overpay for services, expose itself to legal challenge, or be unable to demonstrate value for money. The pattern of expiring contracts and backdated waivers suggests a structural capacity or process failure rather than isolated incidents.
findings.figures: No quantified impact disclosed
findings.quote: Waivers are often driven by late engagement from budget managers and minimal justification, exposing the Council to contractual risk. Contract management suffers from an incomplete register, inconsistent compliance, and lack of systematic performance monitoring, compounded by limitations in the current finance system. Some of these weaknesses have been in place for a number of years and need to be urgently addressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: The shared waste contract with Dover lacks sufficient governance controls to ensure service standards are met.
findings.detail: Folkestone & Hythe has limited authority over the waste management contract, which is managed entirely by Dover. Internal audit identified multiple weaknesses: Veolia self-assesses performance without independent verification and has failed to detect defects; penalty clauses are applied inconsistently; inspections are restricted to weekdays despite weekend service needs. These issues create financial inefficiencies and limit the council's ability to enforce standards.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's major contracts are adequately overseen and whether service failures could result in unbudgeted costs or reputational damage. Shared service arrangements with limited local control are a structural governance risk.
findings.figures: No specific figures on cost impact disclosed
findings.quote: The contract is managed by Dover on behalf of both councils, leaving Folkestone & Hythe reliant on Dover for decisions and oversight. Internal audit identified weaknesses, including Veolia self-assessing performance without detecting defects, ineffective application of penalty clauses, and limited inspections restricted to weekdays despite weekend service needs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: The Princes Parade project has been abandoned with a £3.4m write-off after failing to meet planning consent requirements.
findings.detail: The council is formally closing the Princes Parade scheme and writing off approximately £3.4m in sunk costs in the 2025/26 financial statements. The write-off will be covered by the Financial Stability Reserve. The auditor has raised an improvement recommendation for a lessons learned exercise on project governance.
findings.matters: A £3.4m loss on a capital scheme signals weak project governance or planning assumptions. The scheme ran without formal documentation of the decision, and there is no prior lessons-learned process to prevent similar failures on major capital projects.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: A projected funding gap of £3.6m by April 2028 remains unresolved heading into Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The council has identified a cumulative deficit of £3.6m by 1 April 2028. This issue has now been raised three years running (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25). The auditor notes the council holds £18m in reserves as of 31 March 2025 and has not yet escalated this to a significant weakness, but warns this could change if appropriate steps are not taken to achieve a sustainable financial position before LGR and to transfer appropriate reserves to the successor council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council will hand over a sustainable position to its successor authority in three years, or whether financial pressures will persist. Three consecutive years of the same warning suggests neither savings plans nor structural changes have yet closed the gap.
findings.figures: £3.6m cumulative deficit by 1 April 2028; £18m reserves as at 31 March 2025 (£5.9m general reserves, £15m earmarked)
findings.quote: A medium-term funding gap has been identified, with a projected cumulative deficit of £3.6m by 1 April 2028. The Council must take steps to strengthen its financial position and ensure an appropriate level of reserves is available for transfer to the successor authority ahead of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).
